note: Interference hints shown only after the learner's own error, never before. Written by an AI agent from general knowledge of what English readers tend to expect; not checked by a Hebrew teacher and not tested with learners. Each hint is under 140 characters. 'example' is the worked example shown on a repeated miss. The error kind is inferred from the kind of card or drill item, not diagnosed from what the learner actually said.

kinds.hint: These two letters look alike. Find the one feature that differs, then say the name before you pick.
kinds.example: Bet has a flat base that sticks out to the right; kaf is one smooth curve with no corner. Check the base first.

kinds.hint: A vowel sign is a tiny mark under or beside the letter. Look at its shape and its place before you guess.
kinds.example: Two dots side by side under a letter (tzere) say 'ay'; two dots stacked (shva) are a very short sound or silent.

kinds.hint: Hebrew reads right to left. Start at the right edge of the word and move left, letter by letter.
kinds.example: In שָׁלוֹם start at ש (sh), then ל (l), then ו (o), end at ם (m): sha-lom.

kinds.hint: Alef and ayin carry a vowel but add no consonant sound of their own in everyday Israeli speech.
kinds.example: In אַבָּא only the vowels are heard: a-ba. The first alef just holds the 'a' vowel.

kinds.hint: Five letters change shape at the end of a word. The sound stays the same; only the shape changes.
kinds.example: כ at the start of a word and ך at the end are both kaf: the final one has a long tail down.

kinds.hint: Everyday Hebrew text leaves most vowels out. In this course the marks are shown: read each one in order.
kinds.example: Without marks שלום is just ש-ל-ו-ם; with marks שָׁלוֹם you can read sha-lom.
